content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper utilizes Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) to improve tokenization of
Python code, and introduces a Syntax Aware Transformer architecture to process
the tokenized code. The tokenized code consists of interleaved "content parts"
and "syntax parts", where the content parts are the names of identifiers or
values of literals in the AST, and the syntax parts are the substrings that
surround the content parts in a textual representation of the AST. The tokenizer
deals with identifiers by replacing them with existing names from a name
pool, like replacing student_num with user_defined_var_7, and student_nums with
user_defined_var_8. The AST is used to determine these identifiers to be
replaced. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the APPS
code contest benchmark.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

The proposed method achieves very good performance on the APPS benchmark,
outperforming AlphaCode.

### Weaknesses

Even though the proposed method achieves impressive performance, I have major
concerns about the paper.

There is existing work in the literature both about using AST-s for tokenization
(e.g., [1]), and about replacing identifiers in code with names from a name pool
[2, 3]. The authors were probably not aware of this as it is not addressed in the
paper, which presents these as original contributions without precedent.

As far as I understand [3] handles out-of-vocabulary (OOV) identifiers very
similarly as the present paper and reports considerable accuracy gains (around
6-10%). I believe that this raises the need for an ablation study to determine
which part of the presented result is due to including the ASTs and which part
is due to the name pool.

Similarly, docstring removal is frequently done for tasks which don't require
docstrings, so the effect of it should be measured independently.

My other main concern is about the writing and organization of the paper. Some
of the crucial figures, tables, and algorithms are only present in the Appendix
and are freely referenced in the paper (e.g., the main algorithm in Algorithm 1,
the embedder in Figure 7, or the concrete example on how the input is tokenized
in Table 4).

Section 4.2 about the data augmentation refers to Appendix A.3, which says that
the details are discussed in the Appendix. I couldn't find this discussion. The
part which discusses the Goflec algorithm only reviews the challenges of
designing such an algorithm, and not how the algorithm works. This is also not
described in the Appendix (the algorithm itself is given).

Some of the figures and algorithms are referenced incorrectly, like Algorithm 1
is referenced as Table 1, and Fig. 6 as Fig. 2. I'm not sure about Table 4. All
of these are on page 6.

I also found some smaller issues:
- the Introduction states that perturbing a program written in Python
changes the output more than doing the same to a program in a DSL. Many DSL-s
consist of high-level functional programming constructs where changing something
results in large changes in the output.
- also here, it states that loops and branching are the property of modern
high-level programming languages like Python. I think Fortran and C are
counterexamples.
- in Related Works, Devlin et al. (2017) is given as an example for extending
neural synthesis to general purpose programming languages like Python on the
FlasFill task. The programming language in the FlashFill task is a DSL, not
Python.
- the example of natural language tokenizers tokenizing (cnt=1 vs cnt =   1)
differently. Many tokenizers ignore whitespace, and if we are using one which
doesn't, we can use a pretokenizer.
- the statement that changing the word order does not affect the meaning of a
sentence in natural language. The classic counterexample is "Dog bites man" vs
"Man bites dog".
- Figure 3 is before Figure 2
- there are some small grammar mistakes, like "sythesis" in the second sentence
of the Introduction, the "model design should also be carefully designed" at
the start of Section 4, dor the tenses of the verbs in the first sentence of
the second paragraph on page 8.

[1] Jimenez, M., Maxime, C., Le Traon, Y., & Papadakis, M. (2018, September). On
the impact of tokenizer and parameters on n-gram based code analysis. In 2018
IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME) (pp.
437-448). IEEE.

[2] Gupta, R., Pal, S., Kanade, A., & Shevade, S. (2017, February). Deepfix:
Fixing common c language errors by deep learning. In Thirty-First AAAI
conference on artificial intelligence.

[3] Chirkova, N., & Troshin, S. (2021, June). A Simple Approach for Handling
Out-of-Vocabulary Identifiers in Deep Learning for Source Code. In Proceedings
of the 2021 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for
Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (pp. 278-288).

I have detailed my concerns about the clarity, quality, and novelty in the
Weaknesses section.

I believe that the writing makes it harder to reproduce the paper. For example,
Section 4.1 states that the descriptions are encoded by "two existing pretrained
language models" without naming them. One of them is named in Section 5.2 as
BERT, but I couldn't find the other one.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The presented method achieves very good performance on the APPS dataset.
However, I have major concerns about the causes of these results, the literature
review, the originality of the contributions, and the clarity of the paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new tokenization method for programs for neural sequence-to-sequence learning, by leveraging the syntactic structure of programs. Given a program, the tokenization method parses the program into an AST, and traverses the AST to extract a linearized sequence of syntactic nodes as the tokenization output. During this process, contextual natural language information in the program, such as comments, doc-strings and user-defined identifier names, are removed and canonicalized to indexed placeholders (e.g., `variable_1`). Besides this tokenization strategy, the authors also propose improvements for encoding I/O samples in PBE tasks for Transfromer encoders, by better aligning different elements in I/O samples based on their syntactic roles. This contribution is complementary to the core tokenization method. In experiments, the authors showed that a Tranformer model using the proposed I/O encoding approach and program tokenization method achieves impressive results on the APPs dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength:**

Fusing program-specific syntax into representation learning is an important direction for neural program synthesis
Strong empirical results on the challenging APPs dataset.

**Weaknesses:**

While the empirical results are nice, there are several issues with the technic and the presentation:

* **[Presentation]** There is significant room for improvement for the presentation of this paper. Lots of important technical details are missing or only mentioned in abstract, making it difficult to understand the proposed approach (the figures are pretty nice though). For example, it seems there are two orthogonal contributions in the paper, a tokenization method for programs and a better way to encode I/O samples in input task specification. From Section 3, it is hard to tell which part is corresponding to which of the two contributions. In addition, there is mention of a new “sample-wise attention” mechanism in Section 1, which is not discussed at all later in the main text of the paper. More review comments are in the next section.

* **[Novelty of Syntax-based Tokenization]** If I understand correctly, the core contribution of the tokenization method is to use linearized nodes on the AST of a program (Section 3.2). The high-level idea of this method, to my knowledge, is not novel. There are many prior works using similar ideas of training seq2seq models to predict program AST constructs for code generation (e.g., Yin and Neubig, 2017; Iyer et al., 2018). While these methods do not further canonicalize natural language information in programs as in this submission, the core idea is similar. The authors should discuss those relevant approaches and highlight the differences of their approach.

Additionally, the authors also didn’t discuss recent sub-tokenization methods tailed for code. For example, InCoder (Fried et al., 2022) encodes frequent multi-line program statements in training data as a single token in its vocabulary, which also reduces sequence length. 

Moreover, I am not sure if the idea of removing natural language information from programs during decoding is a good idea. Natural language information could help a model capture the alignments between natural language descriptions and relevant program constructs, which can be helpful for tasks like natural language to program generation. The lack of NL information in the decoder might also explain why using NL descriptions is not helpful in table 2. While the authors mentioned this limitation in Section 6, it should be necessary to conduct more thorough experiments to measure the impact of removing NL information in targets. For example, the authors could add a baseline to table 2 using the same encoder as their proposed model, while the decoder using a sentencepiece model trained on code or the tokenizer in Fried et al., 2022.

* **[Experiment Design]** Only end-to-end results are shown in table 2. There is no baseline using a vanilla transformer with similar size. There are no systematic ablations on different improvements proposed in the model, such as I/O sample encoding, syntax-driven tokenization, data augmentation, etc. Therefore, it’s hard to tell which part contribute the most to the overall result.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clarity is lacking. The proposed `sample-wise` attention mechanism is not discussed in the main text. Section 3.2 is difficult to read. Most technical details are differed to appendix. While there are some examples, there is no **running examples** to help readers understand different components in the proposed approach. I suggest the authors reorganize this section by adding a running example and also provide more high-level technical details using the running example.
content.summary_of_the_review: Good empirical results, but lacking novelty, clarify, and details ablations.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a syntax-aware tokenizer, and uses it to preprocess programs for the Transformer architecture. The main motivation is that code data typically include information that does not change the semantic meaning, including docstring, comments, variable names, etc. Also, existing Transformer tokenizers, which were originally developed for natural language, might break some long variable names into several subtokens, and this also increases the code token length. Therefore, their proposed syntax-aware tokenization includes several steps to standardize the code, including removing docstrings and comments, variable name canonicalization, removing unnecessary whitespaces, etc. They show that their approach achieves good performance on APPS test set, and actually the performance is better without natural language input.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

Designing customized tokenization for code and leveraging the code syntax structure is a promising direction.

Weaknesses:

1. First, the evaluation setting has critical flaws. To make a fair comparison to prior works, the authors should only use APPS training set for training, instead of also using the CodeContests training set. One important reason is because both CodeContests and APPS include competitive programming problems collected from the same websites, it is possible that there is overlap between CodeContests data and APPS test set. Please present results of models trained on APPS training set only.

2. Second, although it is interesting to see that the model without using natural language achieves better performance, I don't think this conclusion generally holds. For example, one limitation of APPS is its high false positive rate due to the small number of I/O pairs per problem, as discussed in [3]. The authors should at least evaluate on another benchmark to validate their claim, e.g., on HumanEval [1], MBPP [2], or CodeContests [3].

3. This work lacks ablation studies to show the effect of different components in their approach. For example, one reason why variable canonicalization is not usually done by prior works on solving coding problems is because it does not improve the performance, so the authors should present results of their approach with variable names preserved. Other necessary ablation studies include the results without data augmentation, encode I/O pairs as a plain sequence instead of using the AST-based tokenizer, etc. Meanwhile, [3] also generates additional I/O, and the paper should discuss how their distribution control process empirically improves the performance.

4. The proposed tokenization algorithm is not technically novel. Variable canonicalization and removing comments have been used as preprocessing steps for some code domains, and [1] modifies their tokenization to reduce the token length of whitespaces.

5. The model architecture is also not novel. The sample encoder and sample-wise attention mechanism were already proposed in [4]. Without empirical comparison, it is hard to see whether AST-based tokenization is necessary for embedding I/O pairs.

6. The writing quality is not good.
i) Many important details are in the appendix, and the main text does not explicitly state that, including the tokenization algorithm and the sample encoder architecture.
ii) On page 15 in the appendix, regarding the step 1 of data generation approach "Guessing of input data candidates", it says that "We discuss this in detail in our Appendix", but there is no more discussion elsewhere.
iii) The authors did not discuss how many samples are included in the augmented training data, and how many I/O pairs are included in each generated problem.
iv) The meaning of first two columns in Table 1 is unclear. Do they refer to the number of I/O pairs and programs for each problem? What does "Count" mean there? I think it is unlikely that the total number of I/O pairs is the same as the total number of programs.

[1] Chen et al., Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code.
[2] Austin et al., Program Synthesis with Large Language Models.
[3] Li et al., Competition-Level Code Generation with Alphacode.
[4] Devlin et al., Robustfill:  Neural Program Learning under Noisy I/O, ICML 2017.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing is unclear, and the quality is not good. It takes multiple passes to get a rough understanding of how their proposed syntax-aware tokenization works, but still some important details are missing.

The proposed approach is not novel enough, and this work does not properly discuss the differences of their design compared to some closely related prior works.

The authors promise to release their code upon paper acceptance.
content.summary_of_the_review: Leveraging the code syntax structures is an important research topic. However, there are important flaws and missing ablation studies in the experiments, and the technical novelty is limited. Also, the writing quality of this submission is not good, and it lacks a proper discussion of related work. Therefore, I recommend a rejection.
